text: Quill the hedgehog had three amber eyes and he used all of them to look for lost things. One morning the weathervane fell off the barn roof and landed in the mud with a big clang. It was Bok-Bok, a rusty tin rooster, and he was very embarrassed. Quill rolled him out of the mud with his nose and it took a long time because Bok-Bok was heavy. Bok-Bok said he could not tell which way the wind went anymore because his tail was bent. So Quill climbed up on the fence and held one paw in the air like a real weather person. The wind is coming from the pond, he said. Bok-Bok crowed a squeaky metal crow that scared two crows away. They banged the bent tail flat with a rock. By lunch Bok-Bok was back on the roof spinning again and Quill went to sleep in the hay.

Marisol found a sheep in the creek behind her house but it was not a normal sheep. It had six legs and its wool was green moss and little white flowers grew in it. She named it Mopsi. Mopsi could not walk on the road because its moss dried out and turned crunchy, so Marisol carried a bucket of creek water everywhere and poured it on Mopsi every twenty minutes. That was a lot of work. At school she hid Mopsi under the stairs and it ate her eraser and half of a library book. The librarian was not happy at all. Marisol had to say sorry and pay for the book with her allowance money. In the end she built Mopsi a wet shady pen next to the creek and visited every single afternoon and the flowers in its wool bloomed all summer.

Grindle was a stone gargoyle on the corner of the old post office and he had one chipped horn and grey wings that were too small for him. He sat still all day because that is the rule for gargoyles. At night he stretched and his shoulders made a sound like two bricks scraping. Grindle wanted to fly but his wings were the size of dinner plates and he weighed as much as a car. He tried jumping off the roof once and made a hole in the flower bed and the gardener never figured out what happened. So Grindle decided he would be good at something else instead. He learned every pigeon by name. There were forty one pigeons. When a pigeon got lost Grindle would call its name in his gravel voice and it would come home, and that was better than flying anyway.

Tuko was a lime green gecko with seven blue stripes down his back and he lived behind the light switch in a kitchen. Everybody in the house heard him at night but nobody ever saw him. Tuko was actually very shy. He counted his stripes every morning to make sure they were all still there because once he had a dream that he woke up plain and grey. One night the little kid of the house left a slice of mango on the table and Tuko went for it. The light snapped on. The kid stared. Tuko froze on the wall with his sticky toes spread out and waited to be screamed at. The kid just pushed the mango closer and turned the light back off. After that Tuko stopped hiding so much, and he let the kid count his stripes, and the kid always got six because Tuko curled the last one under.

Pipit was a paper crane with four wings instead of two because the girl who folded her made a mistake. The other cranes on the shelf laughed at her and said she looked wrong. Pipit did not think she looked wrong. She thought she looked like more crane. One day the window blew open and all the cranes got sucked outside into the wind. The two winged ones spun around and got soggy in a puddle and that was the end of them. Pipit used her extra wings to steer. She flew over the street and over a bus and landed on a windowsill three blocks away. A boy in that house found her and flattened out her creases and put her on his desk. He told everybody who visited that his crane had four wings and it was the only one in the world. Pipit was pretty proud of that.

Sardo was a tin of sardines at the very back of the cupboard and he could talk, which is unusual for a can. He was grumpy about it. His label was faded and his lid was dented in one corner and his expiry date was so old the numbers were rubbed off. Every time somebody opened the cupboard Sardo shouted pick me, pick me, but nobody ever heard him because a can is not loud. He got pushed further back by rice bags and noodles and a jar of pickles that stayed for two years. Then one day there was a big storm and the power went out for four days. The family emptied the whole cupboard looking for food they could eat cold. A hand reached all the way to the back. Sardo held his breath, which cans cannot do, and then he heard the best sound of his life, which was the pull tab going up.

Danilo bought shaved ice from the cart outside the church and when he poured the purple syrup on it a sprite jumped out of the cup. The sprite was small and purple and see through and it had a spoon for a left hand. It said its name was Halo. Danilo dropped the whole cup on the ground which made Halo very upset because that was basically her house. She melted a little bit and got smaller. Danilo panicked and ran to the cart and asked for more ice and the vendor gave him a scoop for free because Danilo looked like he was about to cry. He built the ice back up in a new cup. Halo climbed in and got her size back and even got taller. She lived in the freezer at Danilos house after that and she stirred the water into ice with her spoon hand whenever he asked.

Mister Kettle was a copper kettle with two spouts, one on the left and one on the right, and he was the only kettle in town shaped like that. He could pour two cups at the exact same time. The problem was that he could only make one kind of tea at once, so if two people wanted different tea one of them was going to be disappointed. This caused a lot of arguments in the house. The grandmother wanted ginger and the grandfather wanted plain and they would sit there and glare at each other over the table. Mister Kettle got tired of it. One morning he sat on the stove and boiled and boiled and boiled and would not whistle until they agreed on something. It took an hour. He almost boiled dry. They finally picked ginger for the left spout and ginger for the right spout, and honestly it was pretty good, and after that they always drank the same tea.

Ngiwi was a brown round bird who could not fly and had a long orange beak that curled at the end like a hook. She used the curl to pull worms out of the ground and also to open doors, which the other birds thought was showing off. Ngiwi lived under a fern at the edge of a farm. Every night a fat cat came around and Ngiwi could not fly away from it like a normal bird would, so she had to think instead. She dug a tunnel under the fern with two exits. When the cat came in one end she went out the other end and then she stood behind the cat and honked. The cat hated that. After a week of getting honked at from behind the cat stopped coming, and Ngiwi added a third exit anyway because she was not going to get caught out twice.

Bramblefoot was made out of twigs and dry vine and he was about the size of a badger. He had five ears and they were all leaves, so in autumn his ears turned red and then they fell off and he could not hear anything until spring. That is a hard way to live. He spent every winter feeling around the forest floor with his stick fingers, bumping into rocks. One winter he bumped into a deer that was stuck in a fence. Bramblefoot could not hear the deer crying but he could feel it shaking through the ground. He pulled the wire apart with his hands even though two of his fingers snapped off doing it. The deer got out. In the spring when his leaf ears grew back the first thing Bramblefoot heard was that same deer walking near him every single day, keeping watch, which is a nice thing to hear first.

Tarsi was a little tree creature with enormous round eyes and two long tails that she used like extra hands. Her eyes were so big she could see in the dark better than an owl but in the daytime everything was blinding white so she slept. That meant she never once saw the colour of the forest she lived in. The other night animals told her about green and she did not believe them. One evening there was an eclipse and the sun went dark in the middle of the afternoon. Tarsi woke up confused and climbed out on a branch. She saw the whole valley in grey and blue and dark green and it was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen. It lasted four minutes. Then the sun came back and burned her eyes and she scrambled into her hole. She talked about those four minutes for the rest of her life.

Ate Rina fixed watches in a small shop with a glass counter and one afternoon she opened a broken clock and a brass beetle crawled out. It had eight legs and a key sticking out of its back and it was winding down, walking slower and slower. She wound the key. The beetle stood up straight and clicked at her. She called it Cog. Cog lived in the drawer with the tiny screwdrivers and every morning Ate Rina wound it up before she opened the shop. Cog was good at one thing which was finding dropped springs. A spring from a watch is smaller than a grain of rice and when you drop one it is gone forever. Cog could smell them somehow, or hear them, nobody knew. It would walk across the whole floor and stop and point with one brass leg. Ate Rina saved so much money that she bought a bigger counter.

Puddleback was a fat green toad with nine yellow spots on his back and the spots were arranged exactly like the nine ponds in the valley. He did not know this for most of his life. He just thought he had spots. One dry summer all the ponds started shrinking and the frogs and the fish and the water bugs did not know where to go. An old heron looked down at Puddleback sitting on a rock and said your back is a map. Puddleback twisted around but of course you cannot see your own back. The heron described it to him. Puddleback led everybody from the little ponds that were drying to the two deep ones that were not, and he had to do it from memory because he still could not see his own spots. He got it right anyway. Nine ponds became two ponds that summer, but nothing in them died.

Nimbus Nine was a small grey storm cloud about the size of a dog and he stood on nine raindrop feet. He was assigned to water one hill and that was it. The big clouds got whole cities and mountain ranges and Nimbus Nine got a hill with a goat on it. He was embarrassed to be so small. He tried to make himself look bigger by puffing up and he tried lightning once and it came out as a spark the size of a match. But he was very good at his hill. He knew exactly which patch was dry and he could rain on one square metre without wetting the next one over. During a drought all the big clouds went somewhere else and the hill stayed green, the only green thing anyone could see for miles. The goat lived. That was the whole job and Nimbus Nine did the whole job.

Down where the water is black and cold there was a fish called Sablefin who had three little lanterns hanging off her head. Most fish down there use their lanterns to trick smaller fish into swimming close so they can eat them. Sablefin could not do it. She felt bad every time. So she was hungry all the time and very thin and her three lanterns were dim because she had no energy. Then she noticed something. The shrimp that lived in the cold vents got lost constantly in the dark and drifted away from the warm water and froze. Sablefin started swimming slow circles around the vents with her lanterns on, like a lighthouse. The shrimp followed the light home. They started leaving her the food they could not eat, which was plenty, and her lanterns got so bright that other fish came from far away just to look at her.

Under the bed there was a grey ball of dust and hair and one lost button that served as his eye. He called himself General Lint and he commanded an army of six smaller dust bunnies. Their whole job was to avoid the broom. General Lint had a plan for every situation. When the broom came in from the left they went behind the shoe box. When it came from the right they went under the loose floorboard. He drilled his army twice a day. Then the family got a vacuum. A vacuum does not sweep in from a side, it just arrives, and it is loud, and it does not stop. General Lint lost four of his six soldiers in eleven seconds. He and the last two escaped through a crack into the wall and started over in there, and honestly the wall was better, because a vacuum cannot follow you into a wall.

Nonoy lived on a farm with no animals left because they had all been sold. His lolo welded him a water buffalo out of scrap iron instead. It had a corrugated roof sheet for a back and two curved bicycle handlebars for horns and its name was Bakal. Nonoy did not expect it to move. It moved on the third morning. Bakal walked out to the field on its own and stood in the mud like it knew the job, and it did know the job somehow, and it pulled the plough all day without getting tired or hungry. The neighbours came to watch. Some of them were scared of it. Nonoy walked beside Bakal every day with a rag and wiped the rust off its neck because rust was the only thing that could hurt it. In the wet season he built it a shed before he fixed the hole in his own roof.

Mango was a fruit bat with orange wings the colour of a ripe mango and she had four ears, two big ones on top and two small ones underneath. The extra ears meant she could hear twice as much as any other bat, which sounds great, but a market at noon nearly knocked her out of the sky. She lived in a tree above a busy street and she barely slept. Everybody said just move to the forest. But her tree was the only mango tree for two kilometres and she was not giving it up. Instead she folded her two small ears shut with a bent twig during the day and opened them at night when she needed to hunt. It looked ridiculous. The other bats made fun of the twig. Mango ate the best fruit in the whole province every single night and she did not care what they said.

Snorkel was a dragon made out of a striped sock with two felt horns and a red tongue and one button that did not match the other button. He lived in a toy box. Snorkel believed he was a real dragon and nobody had the heart to tell him otherwise. He practised breathing fire every night and what came out was air, because he was a sock. The other toys were polite about it. Then the baby of the house got a fever and cried for hours and nothing worked. Somebody put Snorkel on their hand and made him roar and breathe pretend fire at the ceiling. The baby stopped crying and laughed so hard she got the hiccups. They did it every night for a week until the fever broke. Snorkel decided that counted as real fire. Honestly it is hard to argue with him about it.

Pebble was a tortoise whose shell was a chipped white teacup with a blue ring painted around it. Nobody knew how that happened, including Pebble. A teacup is not a good shell. It was too shallow so his back legs stuck out, and it had a handle on one side which made him lean, and it was thin enough to crack. He walked in a slow circle for most of his life because of the lean. The other tortoises had proper heavy shells and they told him to be careful all the time and it made him feel small. Then the drought came and every water hole turned to cracked mud. Pebble walked to the last spring, filled his shell to the brim, and walked it back. He did that trip eleven times in two days, leaning the whole way, and the handle was the part everyone held on to when they helped him tip it out.

Lala left the porch light on by accident and in the morning there was a moth on the wall bigger than her hand. Its wings were grey like ash and it had six eyespots on them, three on each side, and the eyespots looked like they were watching you. Lala was not scared. She got a jar. The moth crawled in on its own which was strange. She named it Ashwing and kept it in her room for two days and fed it sugar water on a cotton ball. On the second night she woke up and the six eyespots were glowing faintly, and the pattern of them was the same as the six stars in the window. Lala understood that Ashwing was lost. She carried the jar outside and opened it and pointed it at the sky. Ashwing went straight up until she could not see it anymore and the porch light stayed off forever after that.

Bantay was a street dog with one blue eye and one brown eye and a bent tail from when a tricycle hit him. He guarded a closed hardware store that nobody had opened in three years. There was nothing inside worth guarding. Bantay did not care, it was his store. He slept in front of the roll down door every single night, rain or not, and he barked at anybody who touched it. The neighbours fed him because they felt bad. Then a man came with a key and opened the store for the first time in three years and started cleaning it out. Bantay barked for two hours straight. The man did not chase him off. He put a bowl of water down and kept sweeping. On the day the store reopened Bantay walked inside for the first time in his life and lay down behind the counter like he had always worked there.

Marmalade was a squid the colour of orange jam and she had ten arms like every squid but two of hers were much longer than the rest. She lived near a shipwreck. Squids are supposed to squirt ink and hide when something scary comes, and Marmalade did that for years, but her ink came out pale orange instead of black and it did not hide anything. It just made a little cloud that looked like juice. Everybody could still see her. So she had to learn to be fast instead. She got very good at going backwards through the broken windows of the wreck, which nothing bigger than her could follow her through. One day a diver came down with a torch and found her and she did not run. She squirted her useless orange ink right at his mask and swam off, and he laughed so hard he almost lost his mouthpiece.

Wobblejaw was a round wobbling creature made of blue jelly and he had four jaws arranged around his middle like the petals of a flower. He could chew in four directions at once. That sounds useful and it was, but it also meant he could never keep a secret, because whenever he tried not to say something one of the other three jaws would say it. He lost a lot of friends this way. He tried holding all four shut with his little arms. It did not work. Finally he decided to only listen to secrets he thought people should not be keeping anyway. Somebody in the village was stealing rice from the shared store. Wobblejaw heard about it and by the end of the afternoon all four of his jaws had told the whole street. Everybody was very glad about it and after that they called him the loudest honest thing in the valley.

Tito Ben built a robot the shape of an egg with one round eye in the middle and yellow feet and he named it Sunny-Side. It rolled instead of walking. Sunny-Side had one job which was to bring Tito Ben his coffee in the morning without spilling it. It spilled the coffee every day for four months. Tito Ben kept adjusting things and it kept spilling. He was about to give up. Then he noticed that Sunny-Side was not spilling the coffee at all, it was drinking it, and there was a small hole under the eye nobody had drawn in the plans. Tito Ben did not know how that happened. He gave Sunny-Side its own cup of coffee, a small one, and after that the big cup arrived at the table full and hot and perfectly steady every morning, and the robot rolled a little faster than before.

Perla was eleven and she wanted to enter the town singing contest but she could not read the words on a page fast enough to keep up with the music. Her neighbour Aling Cora was almost eighty and could not hear very well anymore but she had been the town singer forty years ago and she knew every song by heart. They made a deal. Aling Cora sang a line and Perla learned it by ear and sang it back louder so Aling Cora could hear if it was right. They practised on the front steps every afternoon for a month and the whole street got sick of that one song. On the night of the contest Perla forgot the second verse completely. She looked out at the crowd and found Aling Cora in the third row, mouthing it, and she picked it up in time. She got second place. They were both fine with second place.

Jomar was the smallest kid in his class and he was tired of it. He decided he was going to be the best at something that had nothing to do with being tall. He tried running and he was okay. He tried drawing and he was bad. Then his teacher brought in an old broken radio and asked if anybody wanted to take it apart. Jomar took it home and opened it on the kitchen table and spread every piece out on a newspaper so he would remember where they went. It took him two weeks and he did not get it working. He got it working on the third week. After that people started bringing him things. A fan, a rice cooker, two flashlights, a doorbell. His hands were small enough to reach inside things without taking the whole case apart, so being small turned out to be the exact right size.

Aya moved to a new town in the middle of the school year which is the worst time to move. She did not know anybody and everybody already had their group. For two weeks she ate lunch on the low wall behind the canteen by herself and pretended to be busy with her water bottle. She noticed that a girl from another class ate on the other end of the same wall by herself too. Neither of them said anything for four days. On the fifth day it rained and they both ran for the same overhang at the same time and got stuck under it together. Aya said the wall is better. The other girl said the wall is much better. That was the entire conversation. The next day they sat in the middle of the wall instead of the two ends and that was how Aya stopped being new.

Kiko had one job on Saturdays which was to carry the sack of rice home from the market and it was heavier than he was. He tried carrying it on his shoulder and it slid off. He tried dragging it and the bottom wore through. He tried the wheelbarrow and the wheelbarrow had no tyre. So Kiko took his little sisters old stroller, the one with the broken hood, and he cut the seat out and put a board across it. It looked terrible. His cousins laughed at him for six blocks. But he got the whole sack home in one trip without stopping once, and the next Saturday two of those same cousins asked if they could borrow it. He said no. Then he said fine but you have to help me fix the wheel first, and by the end of the month there were three of them on the street.

Basti fished in the shallow part of the river every morning before school and there was always a heron standing there before him. The heron was mud coloured with five long feathers sticking out the back of its neck and it stood on one leg because the other leg was bent the wrong way. Basti called it Mudlark. They were competitors at first. Mudlark took the fish from the good spot near the reeds and Basti got nothing. Then Basti noticed the bent leg meant Mudlark could not wade into the deep channel where the big fish were. So Basti waded out there himself and splashed around and drove the big fish toward the reeds. Mudlark caught two. Basti caught four. They did that every morning for a year and the whole time Basti never got closer than three metres to it, because a heron is still a wild bird and it decides.
